subject: ventures/tax-season-client-picker
professional: an enrolled agent (or small-practice CPA) who runs a solo tax practice and triages late-season and extension-season requests; first checks: is the accept/decline set really deliverable by each deadline and really the most net, is the 'fee to quote' a declined client right, can I enter the work I am already committed to, and does it let me extend (Form 4868 / 7004) instead of only accept or decline

evidence.correctness: Independent recomputation in scratch (scratchpad/tsc/indep.py): exact rational arithmetic, every subset, deliverability decided by simulating the preemptive earliest-due-date schedule day by day (not the engine's cumulative-sum test), ties to fewer hours, own greedy baselines and own forced-inclusion break-even fees. `python3 indep.py fixtures/clients.csv 6` gives best 5 jobs, $3,555, 41 h, $86.71/h; baselines arrival $2,990 (4), fee $3,360 (3), per-hour $3,278 (7); break-evens $485/$810/$1,470/$347/$425: identical to `node cli.mjs plan fixtures/clients.csv --hours-per-day 6` and the guide. With `--hours-per-day 6 --booked 4 --booked-due 2` both give 6 jobs, $3,165, 38 h, baselines $2,575/$2,510/$2,998, break-evens $1,415/$650/$1,370/$292. On 150 random queues (scratchpad/tsc/gen.mjs -> cmp.py, half with booked hours, three capacities) 0 mismatches over 150 plan nets and 266 break-even fees. Raising the C-corp fee to $1,471 makes the CLI accept it (and $486 for the Schedule C), confirming the break-even is the real threshold; at exactly the printed fee it is still declined (strict boundary). The one wrong output found is input handling: `printf 'A big return,$1,200,8,3,40' | node cli.mjs plan - --json` silently reads fee $1, hours 200, due 8, cost 3, note '40' and declines it as 'cannot be finished' rather than raising an error. Not 4: that silent misparse and the strict-boundary wording.
evidence.completeness: Claimed features walked end to end: exact best set (pass), work order with start/finish day and spare hours (pass, hand-checked day 1-2 for 3.5 h after 4 booked hours at 6 h/day), break-even fee per declined client (pass), three baselines (pass), hours already booked and the overbooked warning (pass, CLI run), JSON output (pass), browser page (loaded in headless Chrome via scratchpad/tsc/page.cjs: 'Load worked example' renders the $3,555 summary and five decline rows with $485/$810/$1,470/$347/$425, no console errors), local-only usage counter with opt-out (usage.test.mjs, 9 tests pass), guide page and llms.txt (served copy checked). No stubs or TODOs. Limits (16 engagements, one booked block) are stated.
evidence.verification: `node --test '*.test.mjs'` in the subject root: 32 tests, 32 pass, 0.2 s. Eight seeded mutants via platform/ci/quality_mutate.py: the deadline test in feasible (engine.mjs:105), the pruning test in optimize (engine.mjs:160), the break-even formula (engine.mjs:217) and the schedule start day (engine.mjs:121) are caught; the fewer-hours tie-break (engine.mjs:143), the spare-hours finding threshold (engine.mjs:241), booked hours in the spare capacity (engine.mjs:224) and the zero-net decline reason (engine.mjs:215) survive. The tie test (engine.test.mjs:185) cannot tell the tie-break apart because both tied sets use 8 hours, and the random brute-force check accepts any hours <= the reference (engine.test.mjs:91). The brute-force reference reuses the engine's own feasible() rather than an independent deliverability test. 4 of 8 survived: 2.
evidence.craft: Read engine.mjs (256 lines), cli.mjs (95), index.html script, usage.mjs and the four test files. Pure, dependency-free, small functions, clear comments, exact search with sound pruning, escaped HTML. Defects: CSV split on bare commas (engine.mjs:56) with a dead comma-strip in nonNeg (engine.mjs:42) that can never see a comma, so quoted names and thousands separators fail (one loudly, one silently); an extra positional argument to the CLI is silently ignored (cli.mjs:25); the worked example is duplicated in index.html and fixtures (guarded by page.test.mjs). Acceptable to a senior reviewer with those fixes.
evidence.claims: Checked: 'exact set with the highest total net' (backed: indep.py and engine.test.mjs:81); 'tests check it against every subset' (true, though the reference shares feasible()); 'break-even fee is exact' (backed, but 'would earn a place at a fee of about $X or more' at engine.mjs:219 and 'Worth accepting at' at index.html:75 are off at the boundary: at exactly $X it is still declined); guide numbers $2,990/$3,360/$3,278/$3,555/$86.71/$195 and five break-evens (backed: page.test.mjs and my recomputation); 'nothing is uploaded' (backed: index.html script has no fetch; usage.mjs localStorage only); disclaimer, no-warranty, Circular 230 and competence caveats present on both pages; 'An extension only moves a deadline if it is filed on time, and it does not extend time to pay' matches the IRS Form 4868 instructions. llms.txt in the source points at github.io but `node platform/pages/served-copy.mjs tax-season-client-picker` shows the served copy on marisstella.app with no retired origin, so not a defect.
evidence.fitness: Job walked: a solo EA with ten late requests, 6 h/day, 4 h already committed, pastes the queue and gets which to accept, the order, and the fee to quote. That works for a single queue of up to 16. Gaps a preparer hits in the first hour: work already committed is one block with one due day (engine.mjs:100) when a real book has several committed returns at different deadlines; the decision is modelled as accept or decline, while the common late-season move is to file an extension and do the return later; clients' documents arrive on different days (release dates) and the model lets any return start today; queues over 16 are refused. Usable as a quick decision aid, not as the practice's triage tool.
evidence.domain: Against the scheduling standard: single machine, preemption, deadlines, maximise weighted on-time jobs (1|pmtn|sum w_j U_j); EDD feasibility (Jackson's rule / Horn 1974) is applied correctly and the exhaustive search is exact, and the break-even as best-minus-best-forced is the right shadow price. Against tax practice (IRS Pub 17 / Form 4868 and 7004 instructions on extensions; Circular 230 due diligence noted by the page): the method departs where an EA would look first, the third option of extending (an extension-season deadline is a second due day for the same file, with the value of a later finish and the client's payment-due exposure), and document-arrival dates, neither modelled; README lists extension penalties as out of scope but not the extend-instead choice. Business days counted by the user is acceptable and stated.

defects.what: Rows are split on every comma, so a fee typed '$1,200' silently becomes fee $1, hours 200, due 8, cost 3 and the client is declined as undeliverable with exit 0; a quoted name with a comma is rejected as 'fee must be a number'. The comma strip in nonNeg is dead code that suggests separators were meant to work.

The tie-break test cannot detect the documented fewer-hours rule (both tied sets use 8 hours) and the random brute-force check accepts any hours <= the reference; reversing the tie-break leaves all 32 tests green.

The spare-hours finding is untested with booked hours and at its threshold, and the zero-net decline reason is untested; three mutants there survive. Zero net is also worded 'pays less than its direct costs'.
'would earn a place at a fee of about $X or more' and the page column 'Worth accepting at': at exactly $X the client is still declined (ties go to the current plan); the threshold is strict.

Work already committed is a single block with one due day; a preparer's existing book has several committed returns at different deadlines, which cannot be entered (only approximated by one block or by entering them as jobs the optimiser may drop).

The decision is accept or decline only; the usual late-season third option, file an extension and finish later (second due date, client payment-due exposure), is neither modelled nor listed as a limit, and document-arrival (release) dates are not modelled: every return can start today.
Hard cap of 16 engagements from exhaustive search; an exact pseudo-polynomial DP on half-hour units (Lawler-Moore style) would handle a full queue.
A second positional argument (e.g. two files) is silently ignored; only the first file is planned.

verdict: The arithmetic is right: my own exact-rational subset search with a day-by-day EDD simulation reproduces the worked queue ($3,555 over 41 h, baselines $2,990/$3,360/$3,278, break-evens $485/$810/$1,470/$347/$425), the booked-hours variant, and 150 random queues with 266 break-even fees with no mismatch, and the browser page renders the same. It misses the bar on verification: 4 of 8 seeded mutants survive, including a reversed tie-break that the tie test was written to catch but cannot. For an enrolled agent the method is sound scheduling math but thin practice: one committed-work block, no extend-instead option, no document-arrival dates, and a silent misparse of '$1,200'. Usable as a quick decision aid for one small queue; not yet a triage tool a practitioner would rely on.
